cls: Substituted benzamide / dopamine D2 receptor antagonist (prokinetic, antiemetic)
pharm: Clebopride is a substituted benzamide and selective dopamine D2 receptor antagonist with prokinetic and antiemetic properties, structurally and pharmacologically related to metoclopramide. By blocking peripheral D2 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract it enhances gastric and upper intestinal motility and accelerates gastric emptying, while central D2 blockade in the chemoreceptor trigger zone contributes to its antiemetic effect. Because it crosses the blood-brain barrier and blocks central dopamine receptors, it shares the extrapyramidal, tardive dyskinesia and hyperprolactinemia liability of other benzamide prokinetics.

Avoid; excretion in milk not characterized
Use with caution; reduce dose in impairment
Use with caution; reduce dose in impairment
summary: Clebopride is a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist of the substituted benzamide class used as a prokinetic and antiemetic for dyspepsia and nausea/vomiting in countries where it is marketed. The usual adult dose is 0.5 mg three times daily taken before meals. It is NOT FDA-approved; the information below is based on non-FDA sources (EMA/national SmPC and BNF-type references). Like metoclopramide, it carries risks of extrapyramidal reactions, tardive dyskinesia and hyperprolactinemia, so treatment should be short-term and at the lowest effective dose.
indications: Symptomatic treatment of dyspepsia and functional gastrointestinal motility disorders (e.g. postprandial fullness, bloating, epigastric discomfort)
Nausea and vomiting of various causes where a dopamine antagonist antiemetic is appropriate
Delayed gastric emptying and disorders associated with impaired upper gastrointestinal motility

dosage.n: Take about 15-30 minutes before each main meal
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
Increased risk of accumulation and extrapyramidal effects

dosage.d: Limit total daily dose and treatment duration
dosage.n: Minimize duration to reduce tardive dyskinesia risk

admin: Take orally 0.5 mg three times daily before meals (approximately 15-30 minutes before eating)
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary
Reassess the need for continued therapy and discontinue if no benefit
Discontinue immediately if abnormal involuntary movements or other extrapyramidal signs appear
moa: Clebopride antagonizes dopamine D2 receptors. In the gastrointestinal tract, peripheral D2 blockade removes dopaminergic inhibition of cholinergic activity, increasing lower esophageal sphincter tone, enhancing gastric and small-bowel motility and accelerating gastric emptying (prokinetic effect). Centrally, D2 antagonism in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the area postrema produces an antiemetic effect. Central dopamine blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway accounts for extrapyramidal reactions, and blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin secretion.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to clebopride or other substituted benzamides
Gastrointestinal mechanical obstruction, perforation or hemorrhage
Confirmed or suspected extrapyramidal disorder or history of tardive dyskinesia from benzamides/neuroleptics
relative: Parkinson's disease (dopamine blockade may worsen symptoms)
Epilepsy or conditions lowering seizure threshold
Children (avoid; high risk of extrapyramidal reactions)
monitor: Concomitant antipsychotics or other dopamine antagonists (additive extrapyramidal risk)
Anticholinergic or opioid co-medication (antagonize prokinetic effect)

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established; avoid use during pregnancy unless the potential benefit clearly outweighs the risk. As a dopamine antagonist, neonatal extrapyramidal effects are a theoretical concern with exposure near term.
lact: Excretion of clebopride in human milk has not been adequately characterized; as with related benzamides it may pass into milk and increase prolactin. Avoid use during breastfeeding or discontinue nursing.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; reduce the dose and/or dosing frequency because reduced clearance may increase exposure and the risk of extrapyramidal effects.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; clebopride undergoes hepatic metabolism, so reduce the dose in significant liver dysfunction and monitor for adverse effects.

major: Antipsychotics / neuroleptics and other dopamine antagonists - additive risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia
Levodopa and dopamine agonists - mutual antagonism reduces efficacy of both
moderate: Anticholinergic agents - antagonize the prokinetic (gastric motility) effect
Opioid analgesics - oppose gastrointestinal prokinetic effect and add CNS depression
CNS depressants, sedatives and hypnotics - additive sedation
Drugs whose absorption depends on gastric emptying rate - altered absorption from accelerated transit
minor: No clinically significant CYP-mediated interactions well established
interactions.food: Take before meals; food intake is part of the dosing schedule rather than a contraindication.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; additive central nervous system depression and sedation.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum prolactin and can interfere with the interpretation of prolactin-based diagnostic tests; may briefly raise serum aldosterone.

common: Galactorrhea, breast tenderness or menstrual changes (hyperprolactinemia)
serious: Tardive dyskinesia, especially with prolonged use
emergency: Acute dystonic reaction (oculogyric crisis, trismus, laryngospasm)
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness)

monitoring: Extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, abnormal involuntary movements)
Signs of tardive dyskinesia with longer-term use
Serum prolactin if galactorrhea, gynecomastia, amenorrhea or sexual dysfunction occur
Mental status and sedation, particularly in the elderly
counsel: Take one tablet before each main meal, three times a day, exactly as prescribed
This medicine can cause drowsiness; do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol while taking this medicine
Seek urgent medical attention if you develop abnormal muscle movements, stiffness, tremor, restlessness, or twisting of the face, neck or eyes
Report breast swelling, milk discharge, or menstrual changes to your doctor
Do not use for longer than prescribed and do not use during pregnancy or breastfeeding unless advised
pk: Prokinetic effect within about 30-60 minutes of an oral dose
Plasma concentration approximately 1-2 hours after oral dose
Several hours; three-times-daily dosing maintains effect
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from moisture and light
pearls: NOT FDA-approved; marketed in some countries (e.g. Spain, Italy, parts of Asia). Information here is based on non-FDA sources (EMA / national SmPC and BNF-type references), not an FDA label.
Substituted benzamide and dopamine D2 antagonist closely related to metoclopramide, sharing extrapyramidal, tardive dyskinesia and hyperprolactinemia risks
Use short-term and at the lowest effective dose to minimize the risk of tardive dyskinesia
Acute dystonic reactions are more frequent in children, young adults and the elderly; avoid in children
Anticholinergics and opioids blunt the prokinetic effect, while concomitant antipsychotics increase extrapyramidal risk
Antagonizes levodopa and dopamine agonists - avoid in Parkinson's disease
Acute extrapyramidal reactions usually respond to anticholinergics (e.g. biperiden) or antihistamines
missed: Take the missed dose before the next meal when you remember. If it is nearly time for the next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue the regular before-meal schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, confusion and pronounced extrapyramidal reactions (dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism). Management is supportive and symptomatic; extrapyramidal symptoms can be treated with anticholinergic antiparkinsonian agents (e.g. biperiden) or antihistamines, with monitoring of vital signs and airway protection. There is no specific antidote.
